questions.stem: A market analyst is preparing for a quarterly planning meeting and asks Claude about a competitor's company structure, which was set out in a public filing two years ago and has not changed. Research is switched off in her chat, and she has 15 minutes before the meeting. What is the MOST appropriate approach?

options.text: Switch Research on, because every answer about a company should be researched to be safe.
Ask it in the chat as it stands, and note in the minutes that the structure should be re-checked against the filing before it is relied on.
Switch Research on and ask it to find the most recent filings, in case the structure has changed since then.
Open a new Project, upload the filing, and rebuild the answer as a reusable artifact.

questions.explanation: Research earns its cost on **information that changes** — prices, headcounts, leadership, product availability, anything current. A two-year-old, unamended public fact is the case where research adds time and a pile of citations without adding knowledge, and where a normal chat answer is appropriate. Stating the source so it can be checked in a minute is a sensible habit that costs nothing. Note how the other options misread the situation: option A applies research as a general safety rule rather than a fit-for-purpose tool, option C re-introduces the cost it was trying to avoid by researching a settled fact, and option D builds a reusable system for a one-off question.

whyWrong.A: Treating Research as a default safety measure is both slower and less useful than it sounds. When a fact is stable and documented, extra searching mostly produces more material she has no time to read.
whyWrong.C: She has already established the structure is unchanged since the filing, so searching for later filings cannot change the answer. The time saved by staying in chat is the whole point of the judgement.
whyWrong.D: A Project and an artifact are for work that repeats or must be shared and edited by others. One question in one meeting does not justify a reusable setup, and she does not have the time to build it.

questions.mindset: Use research when the information changes; use a normal chat when the fact is stable, documented and checkable.

questions.stem: A freelance communications consultant runs 12 client projects a year. She has three things she wants Claude to remember: her preferred structure for a media briefing, the house voice for each of two clients that must never be mixed up, and the fact that she prefers short paragraphs. She has currently written all three into her account-wide personalisation. What is the MOST accurate description of how these should be organised?

options.text: Personalisation should hold the two client voices and the Projects should hold her briefing structure, since client voice is the more important of the three.
All three belong in personalisation, because personalisation is the feature designed to remember things between chats.
Personalisation suits her own cross-client working habits; each client's voice belongs in a Project for that client, so the two are kept apart and applied automatically whenever she works in it.
All three belong in memory, because memory applies across every conversation automatically.

questions.explanation: The three features have different **scopes**, and choosing correctly is mostly a question of scope. Personalisation is the right home for her own working habits, because they genuinely apply everywhere — a preference for short paragraphs is hers, not a client's. Client voice is different in kind: it is specific, it is confidential, and it must never travel between clients, so it belongs in a Project dedicated to that client, where it is applied automatically on every chat in that Project. Memory sits between them and is designed for personal preferences and facts about the user rather than client-specific working rules. The trap is the assumption that one feature should hold everything because it is the one you already know.

whyWrong.B: Putting client voices in account-wide personalisation is the exact failure she is trying to avoid: both clients' tone rules apply to every chat, on every project, with nothing to stop them leaking into each other's work.
whyWrong.D: Memory is built for personal context about the user across her own conversations. It is not a place to keep a client's confidential brand guidance, and it is not a mechanism for applying rules to a specific piece of work.
whyWrong.A: It inverts the priority logic. What must be kept apart is the client-specific material, so that is what needs a boundary; her own structural preference would not cause a cross-client error if it appeared everywhere.

questions.mindset: Personalisation is for your own habits across chats; a Project is the boundary that keeps client-specific rules apart.

questions.stem: A law firm's paralegal builds a clause library in Claude as an artifact: a structured document of standard clauses she can click through and copy from. The firm's practice manager now wants to use the same library in Word, add her own track changes and circulate it to fee-earners for comment. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: Share the artifact with the practice manager's Claude account so she can edit it there and export it later.
Ask Claude to turn each clause into a separate small artifact so they can be combined in any order in Word.
Keep the artifact as the master copy, ask the practice manager to suggest changes in a chat, and have the paralegal apply them by hand each time.
Ask Claude to produce the clause library as a file she can download, since the content is finished and the editing will happen in Word by people who do not use Claude.

questions.explanation: Artifacts are built for **working inside Claude** — iterating with Claude in the conversation, editing the document in place, and sharing it with other Claude users. They are not the right home for a document whose lifecycle has moved to another tool and to people who are not in Claude at all. Option A matches the deliverable to the workflow: the content is settled, the editing and commenting happen in Word, and the fee-earners need a file. The important judgement is noticing that the *stage* of the work has changed — an artifact that was ideal while drafting becomes the wrong container once the document is handed to a wider group for tracked changes. Options B and D both keep people inside Claude for no benefit, and option C fragments the library without solving the editing problem.

whyWrong.A: Sharing the artifact only helps people who use Claude. The practice manager's actual need is Word track changes with fee-earners, so moving the file across tools is the requirement, not an obstacle.
whyWrong.B: Splitting the library into separate artifacts adds administration and still leaves the editing problem in place. It does not produce a Word file that fee-earners can comment on.
whyWrong.C: Manual re-application on every change is the manual process the artifact was meant to remove, and it introduces exactly the transcription errors that a shared file avoids.

questions.mindset: When the editing and the audience move outside Claude, deliver a file — artifacts are for working inside the conversation.

questions.stem: A finance analyst has a weekly task: summarise the previous week's figures from a workbook her team maintains in the company shared drive, then write three paragraphs of commentary. Today she downloads the file and pastes it into a fresh chat each Monday. Last month's commentary contained a figure that was superseded two weeks before she pasted it, because she had copied from an earlier download. What is the MOST effective improvement?

options.text: Paste the file again each week but ask Claude to check the file's modification date first and warn her if it looks old.
Ask Claude to write the three paragraphs first and insert the figures afterwards, so the writing does not wait on the data.
Connect the shared drive to her workspace where the organisation has enabled it, so each run reads the current file rather than a copy she chose days earlier.
Keep a copy of the correct figures at the end of each chat as a reminder for the following week.

questions.explanation: The error was not a prompting error at all — it was a **staleness error**, caused by working from a copy chosen days earlier. The fix belongs where the staleness comes from. Where a connector is available and approved, each run reads the current file, so a later correction by her team is picked up automatically and the failure mode cannot recur. This is worth noting as a product-judgement question rather than a technical one: choosing between pasting, connecting and persisting is a decision about where the source of truth should sit. The distractors all leave the copy step intact, which is the actual cause. Note that this is a different situation from the occasional one-off upload of a document Claude has no other access to, where pasting is entirely appropriate.

whyWrong.A: A modification-date warning is useful but it depends on her remembering to notice it, and it still requires her to download and paste. It adds a check to a process whose root problem is working from a stale copy.
whyWrong.B: Separating prose from data removes the writing bottleneck but not the risk. The same stale file would still be the source of the figures, and writing first makes it more likely the numbers are fitted to prose already written.
whyWrong.D: Keeping reminders in the chat adds a second copy to become stale. The commentary still originates from a file downloaded on a particular day, and next Monday's version inherits last Monday's figure.

questions.mindset: When the error is a stale copy, fix where the data comes from, not how carefully you prompt.

questions.stem: An analyst must publish a competitive brief every Monday. It combines public information about three competitors with figures from the company's own CRM export, uses the same nine-section structure every week, and must make clear which statements come from which source. She has built it ad hoc so far and last week's version quoted a CRM figure from the wrong month. Which TWO changes BEST fit this recurring job? Choose TWO.

options.text: Put the CRM export, the section structure and the writing rules in a Project, so every weekly run starts from the same material and the same format without her re-explaining them.
Save the CRM figures in memory, so they are available automatically in every chat she starts.

Use Research for the public material, and instruct it to keep published figures and internal figures in separate labelled parts, to flag anywhere the two contradict each other, and to date every published figure.
Ask Claude at the start of each week to 'be careful with figures' and to double-check them before writing.
Build an artifact for the brief so it can be shared read-only with the leadership team, who need to view it but not change it.

questions.explanation: Recurring work needs the **repeated instructions and sources in one persistent place**, and the two correct options split the job along its real fault lines. Option A fixes the error that actually occurred: the wrong-month figure came from material being re-supplied by hand each week with no fixed reference point, so a Project that carries the current export and the house structure removes that whole class of mistake and makes the weeks comparable. Option C addresses the second requirement, **provenance** — separating published from internal figures, flagging contradictions between them and dating every published figure are what let a reader tell evidence from assertion, and they turn 'which source is this?' from a research task into a visible property of the document. Options B and D add nothing reliable: memory is not a place for a weekly data feed, and asking for care is not a control.

whyWrong.B: Memory is built for personal context, not for a weekly data feed or for material that must be shared with a team. Nothing would keep the CRM figure current, and nothing would stop it being carried into a draft for the wrong week.
whyWrong.D: Asking Claude to be careful is not a mechanism. The wrong-month figure was a sourcing error, and an instruction to check figures does not make Claude fetch the file that was correct rather than the one at hand.
whyWrong.E: A shareable artifact is a reasonable container for the finished brief, but it does not fix either underlying problem. The wrong figure and the mixed provenance would both survive, because the error happened before the document was rendered.

questions.mindset: Recurring jobs belong in a Project for the repeated sources and rules; provenance has to be designed in, not added later.

questions.stem: A team lead is writing a one-page note to help colleagues choose between Claude's model tiers. She asks you which of the following statements are accurate. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.text: Each tier has a different context limit, so a long document must be handled with the most capable tier.
Cheaper and faster models are designed for simple tasks and should not be used on anything a business will act on.
A larger, more capable model knows more about recent events, so it gives better answers about last month's news.
A new release within a tier is generally better at the same price than the older release it replaces, so a capability gap recorded months ago may no longer hold.

questions.explanation: Three misunderstandings come from confusing **capability with knowledge**. Recency is not something a bigger model buys: every tier has the same training cut-off, which is exactly why web search or Research exists for current information. Context limits are a property of the product and plans rather than of the tier, so a long document does not force an upgrade. And the notion that lighter tiers are unsuitable for consequential work is simply false — well-specified extraction, classification and routine drafting are precisely what fast tiers handle well, which is why using the strongest tier for everything is both slower and costlier. The correct statement is the one that puts the emphasis where it belongs: on re-testing rather than on inherited reputation.

whyWrong.C: This is the most common misconception and it is worth being precise about it. A more capable model reasons better over what it knows; it does not know what happened more recently. For current information you need search or Research.
whyWrong.A: Context limits are not tier-specific, and document length is a poor reason to choose a tier in any case. How well the model reasons over a long document, and what structure you give it, matter much more than raw length.
whyWrong.B: This overstates the division between tiers and, practically, invites the pattern the exam cares about: an expensive tier used for work that does not need it, exhausting usage limits while adding little quality.

questions.mindset: Capability is reasoning quality over known information — it is not recency, not context length, and not a reason to use the top tier everywhere.

questions.stem: A council revenue team must sort about 6,000 inbound enquiries a year into six categories, using a written definition for each. Around 4% of items are unclear or contain two categories. She works in Claude's chat interface with no developer support, and has until the end of the quarter. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Run the batch on the fastest tier against the written definitions, then work through the items it flags as unclear herself, using the strongest tier to help reason about the difficult ones.
Run the whole batch on the most capable tier, since a wrong category can affect a customer's council tax.
Run the batch on the fastest tier and accept its answer for every item, since it completed the batch a long way inside the deadline.
Ask Claude which single tier is best for categorisation, then use that tier for every future task of any kind.

questions.explanation: This is the case where **the workload, not the stakes in the abstract, decides the tier**. A category set defined in writing is a bounded classification task — high volume, repeated, with a checkable definition — which is what fast tiers handle reliably and quickly. But the honest design also includes the 4%: asking Claude to flag anything ambiguous converts the residue into a small, human work queue instead of a silent 4% error rate, and those few items are exactly where stronger reasoning earns its cost. That combination matches her real constraints: no developer support, a fixed deadline and a need to be able to explain the process. Note the pattern in the wrong answers — using the strongest tier on everything, accepting output to hit a deadline, or turning one good choice into a universal rule.

whyWrong.B: The most capable tier on 6,000 items spends the strongest capability where the task is routine and returns capacity that could have gone to the 4% of genuinely hard cases. Stakes alone do not make a well-defined classification difficult.
whyWrong.C: Finishing early is not a quality control. Accepting every classification without review means a 4% error rate becomes a 240-item backlog of mis-routed enquiries, discovered by customers rather than by the team.
whyWrong.D: One good decision about a bounded classification says nothing about the next task, which may need speed, or depth, or neither. Generalising a tier choice is how teams end up paying for capability they are not using.

questions.mindset: Pick the tier from the task's difficulty, then route the hard residue to a stronger tier and a human.

questions.stem: An HR business partner asks Claude to compare two versions of a redundancy policy and identify every point where they interact in a way that creates a new obligation. She pastes both policies but leaves out the related enhanced-settlement agreement, which the previous version's obligations depend on. The analysis misses three interactions, and she wants to try again this week. What is the MOST sound advice?

options.text: Switch to the most capable tier and ask it to be more thorough about interactions between the documents.
Add the enhanced-settlement agreement to the materials, restate what she is looking for, and use the strongest tier available for this kind of cross-document reasoning.
Ask for the analysis twice in fresh chats and see which version finds more interactions.
Ask Claude to list what other documents it would need, and use its suggestions as the scope for the analysis.

questions.explanation: This is a **missing-input failure wearing a capability costume**, and it is worth naming precisely because the instinctive response is to upgrade the model. The three missed interactions are all interactions with a document Claude has never seen; no amount of reasoning recovers an input that was not supplied, and a more capable model will produce a more confident analysis of an incomplete set. The fix is therefore twofold and in this order: **add the missing agreement and restate the question**, then use strong capability for the genuinely hard part — reasoning across three interacting documents, where errors are expensive and hard for her to spot. Option A gets the second half right and the first half wrong, which is why the failure repeats.

whyWrong.A: A larger model applied to incomplete inputs produces a better-reasoned account of the wrong problem. She would get a confident, well-reasoned analysis that is still missing the three interactions she needs.
whyWrong.C: Two samples of the same incomplete input tell her about run-to-run variation, not about what was left out. Both runs will agree that the two policies interact in the ways they can see.
whyWrong.D: Letting Claude set the scope of a legal analysis removes the domain judgement from the person who is accountable for it. Its suggestions may be useful as a checklist, but the scope has to be decided by someone who knows which agreements govern.

questions.mindset: A missing input is not a missing capability — add the document before you upgrade the model.

questions.stem: A head of legal services argues that the firm should put every legal task on the most capable tier, because 'a mistake in this department costs more than the licences will'. Her team runs about 40 routine drafting tasks a week alongside three high-value matters a quarter, and the team's usage allowance runs out by Wednesday. Which TWO statements would be accurate pushback? Choose TWO.

options.text: A higher tier does not remove the need for review, so the accountability argument does not support defaulting to the most capable tier.
For well-specified drafting against known precedents, extra capability often buys little, while the cost and latency apply to every task, so the capability should follow the task.
Running out of allowance mid-week is not connected to model choice, so it is irrelevant to this decision.
Routine drafting should be handled without any human review, because a faster model removes the need to check the work.
A licence cost is small next to the cost of a single legal error, so cost should not enter the decision at all.

questions.explanation: The head of legal services is making a **real argument from a real risk**, and the useful response does not dismiss it — it identifies where it stops applying. Option A draws the line correctly: higher capability does not transfer accountability, so a stronger model does not reduce the need for a lawyer to sign off, which means the risk argument cannot be settled by model choice. Option B addresses the actual distribution of work: roughly forty routine tasks a week against three matters a quarter is a case for matching capability to task, and because cost and latency apply to every single request, the premium is paid on the routine ones too. The other three are wrong in instructive ways — allowance consumption is directly a model-choice consequence, 'no review' is the opposite of safe, and a single catastrophic error is not a sound basis for discarding operating costs.

whyWrong.C: Usage allowance consumption is one of the most direct consequences of tier choice, since the more capable tier costs more per request and consumes the allowance faster. Running out by Wednesday is a symptom of exactly this decision.
whyWrong.D: Nothing about a faster model removes the need for a qualified person to check the work. Removing review on 40 tasks a week in a legal department is the change most likely to produce the error she is trying to prevent.
whyWrong.E: This treats expected cost as if it were dominated by one rare outcome. The routine tasks happen forty times a week, so their cost accumulates continuously while the large losses are, by definition, rare and not priced in by ignoring cost.

questions.mindset: Higher capability does not transfer accountability, and it does not make routine work better; capability should follow the task.

questions.stem: A recruitment coordinator must check 200 first-round interview notes for one thing only: whether each candidate mentioned salary expectations. It is a yes-or-no question against a clear rule, the notes average 200 words, and she needs the answer before interviews start at 2 p.m. A colleague recommends the most capable tier because 'getting this wrong ruins a candidate's experience'. What is the BEST assessment?

options.text: The colleague is right, because consequences for candidates are severe and the most capable tier is warranted at any cost.
The task is bounded and repetitive with a single clear criterion, so a fast tier is the right starting point and she should spot-check a sample to see whether it holds.
She should ask the fastest tier, then send every result to the most capable tier to confirm it, which removes the risk entirely.
She should ask the fastest tier for the list of candidates who did not mention salary, and read those 200 notes herself.

questions.explanation: The judgement being tested is that **consequence and task difficulty are different things**, and a single clear criterion over short, uniform documents is about as easy as this work gets. A fast tier with a written rule is the appropriate starting point, and — crucially — she verifies rather than assumes: checking a sample of the notes against Claude's answers tells her whether the cheap approach holds for her data, which is evidence rather than optimism. Option D is a neat trick with the same insight but an impractical workload, since reading 200 notes is the task she was trying to avoid. Options A and C both misfire on the same principle: severity justifies care, not indiscriminate use of the strongest capability, and running every answer through two tiers removes neither the verification nor the cost.

whyWrong.A: Severity does not make a well-defined lookup hard. The colleague is arguing from the stakes to the capability, and the middle step — how hard the task actually is — is the one that determines the tier.
whyWrong.C: Escalating every item to a stronger tier spends the expensive step on the whole batch, so it has the same cost problem as just using that tier throughout, with extra steps and no independent check.
whyWrong.D: Reading 200 short notes to verify 200 yes-or-no answers is a manual verification burden of the same order as the original reading task. Checking a sample gives her the same decision with a fraction of the effort.

questions.mindset: Judge tiers by task difficulty, then verify a sample — severity alone is a reason for care, not for the top tier.

questions.stem: A product manager is briefing colleagues on how to choose between Claude's tiers for a piece of work, and asks which requirement maps to which decision. Which mapping is MOST accurate?

options.text: If people are waiting for the answer during a call, start from the fastest tier and test that quality holds. If quality per item matters most and the volume is low, use the strongest tier.
If people are waiting for the answer during a call, use the strongest tier to be safe. If quality matters most, use the fastest tier and check every result.
If volume is high, use the strongest tier so each item is done properly. If volume is low, speed is all that matters.
If the work is confidential, use the fastest tier so less data is processed. If the work is routine, use the strongest tier to build capability.

questions.explanation: Model choice is a **trade-off between three named requirements — speed, cost and quality per item — plus the volume at which they apply**, and each of them has a different lever. Latency is dominated by tier, so when a person is waiting, the fast tier is the starting point and the only question is whether its quality holds for the actual task. Quality per item is where the strongest tier earns its cost, and it is affordable precisely because volume is low. The other mappings get the trade-off backwards in ways that are common in practice: they treat the strongest tier as universally safe and the fastest as a stopgap, when in reality the two requirements pull in opposite directions and must be weighed against each other.

whyWrong.B: This inverts both levers. It pairs the strongest tier with the requirement it is worst at (latency) and the fastest tier with the requirement it is weakest at (quality), then proposes checking every result, which is a cost with no ceiling.
whyWrong.C: High volume is precisely the case for the cheaper, faster tier, because the per-item cost is multiplied thousands of times. And low volume is exactly when the strongest tier is affordable, so low volume making speed the only consideration is backwards.
whyWrong.D: Confidentiality is a data-handling question governed by your workspace, agreements and policy — not a function of which tier you choose. It does not follow that faster models process less data, and routine work is precisely where fast tiers perform well.

questions.mindset: Match the tier to the binding requirement and the volume: latency pulls down, per-item quality pulls up, volume decides what you can afford.

questions.stem: A finance analyst must compare a 14-page proposed outsourcing contract against the current 22-page agreement and identify every place where the new terms interact with existing obligations to create a new liability. She does this about four times a year, the budget for model usage is not a constraint, and the findings go into a recommendation the board will rely on. What is the MOST appropriate choice?

options.text: Use the fastest tier, since this happens only four times a year and quality is not important for a low-volume task.

Use the strongest tier, with a structured prompt that sets out the documents, what counts as an interaction creating a new obligation, and the format of the output, and plan on reviewing the findings rather than reading them as final.
Use the fastest tier but ask it three times and keep the longest answer, since a longer answer is more thorough.
Use whichever tier is available fastest, since a contract review is fundamentally a reading task and all tiers read equally well.

questions.explanation: Three features of this task point the same way, and it is worth seeing them as one decision. **Low volume** means the strongest tier's per-item cost is irrelevant — four uses a year cost almost nothing. **High consequence** means a missed interaction between clauses has legal and financial effect, and the board will not be able to spot a subtle miss. **The difficulty is reasoning, not reading**: identifying where two documents combine to create an obligation the drafters did not write down is exactly the class of work where capability matters. Option B also keeps responsibility where it belongs — the structure of the prompt and the review afterwards. Notice that the low-volume, high-consequence combination is the clearest case for the strongest tier, and it is the one situation where cost arguments genuinely do not apply.

whyWrong.A: Low volume is an argument for the strongest tier, not against it. When a task happens a handful of times a year, per-item cost is close to irrelevant, so quality should decide.
whyWrong.C: Longest is not thoroughest — repeated generation produces variations, and length here would mostly reflect repetition. Asking the same model three times gives three samples of the same capability, not more of it.
whyWrong.D: All tiers can read the documents; they do not reason over their interaction identically. Collapsing 'reading' and 'reasoning' is the error that makes difficult analytical work look like a simple extraction job.

questions.mindset: Low volume plus high consequence is the clearest case for the strongest tier, and cost arguments do not apply there.

questions.stem: A data team's managers upgraded their plan and instructed everyone to use the strongest tier, hoping it would fix the quality of a weekly risk summary. The summaries are no better. She suspects the real problem: the prompt they all paste in is 25 pages of accumulated context — five years of policy changes, three naming conventions, two contradictory definitions of a customer segment and a long list of example summaries — and the instruction 'summarise the risks for this week'. Which TWO responses are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Establish whether the failure is in the inputs or in the output, by testing a short prompt with the current week's data on a smaller set of cases and seeing whether quality improves.

Split the accumulated context into a small set of explicit instructions for the summary task, keep the long material available as a reference rather than in every message, and resolve which definition of a customer segment is current.
Buy additional seats so each manager can run the same prompt several times and keep the best result.
Roll back to the previous model version, since the upgrade is the only change made in the same period as the change in output quality.
Ask the team to add 'be thorough and precise' to the end of the prompt, since the current instruction is too brief.

questions.explanation: When quality does not improve after moving to the strongest tier, the **tier was probably never the binding constraint**, and the disciplined move is to test that rather than escalate again. Option A does this cheaply and honestly: a short prompt on a small set of real cases shows whether the inputs or the model are responsible, and it produces evidence rather than another opinion. Option B then does the actual work — the 25-page context contains two contradictory segment definitions, and no amount of reasoning produces a stable answer from contradictory inputs. Reducing the pasted context to explicit task instructions, keeping the long material available as a reference rather than in every message, and settling which definition is current addresses the three defects the situation contains. Note that all three remain true even if the tier is right: better reasoning over contradictory context still yields contradictory output.

whyWrong.C: More seats and repeated runs scale the input problem. Every run would carry the same contradictory definitions, and the team would burn allowance producing variations on a defective prompt.
whyWrong.D: Correlation with the upgrade is not a reason. Output quality was unchanged, which is the observation that undercuts this explanation rather than supporting it, and reverting adds a variable instead of removing one.
whyWrong.E: The instruction is not the problem; the inputs are. Adding an emphasis about thoroughness to a prompt containing two contradictory definitions mostly produces longer answers that resolve the contradiction differently each week.

questions.mindset: If a tier change did not fix quality, test the inputs before escalating again.

questions.stem: A finance team moved its monthly variance commentary to the strongest tier available, hoping the quality would justify the cost. The reasoning and wording are now consistently better, but every month the published commentary contains one arithmetic error that takes an afternoon to trace. Each error is in a simple calculation Claude performed while writing, such as a percentage variance across two figures in the source table. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: Move to the most capable tier available, in case arithmetic is one of the areas it still struggles with.

Keep the tier that improved the writing, and change the workflow: have Claude output the figures it used in a small table for a person to verify, or compute the derived numbers elsewhere and have it use only those values.
Ask Claude to double-check its own arithmetic before presenting the commentary, and rely on that step.
Ask Claude to round all percentages to one decimal place and to flag any figure it is not confident about.

questions.explanation: There is now a **separate capability problem from the tier decision**, and conflating them is what caused the endless shopping. The strongest tier demonstrably fixed the writing — that choice was right, and reversing it would give back a real gain. The residual error is different in kind: calculating a percentage while composing prose is a step that no model should be trusted with silently, because it cannot be checked against anything in the output. Option B removes the unreliable step rather than exhorting against it — either the derived figures are computed by something deterministic and Claude works from them, or they are surfaced in a table where a person verifies them in a couple of minutes. Note that asking for self-checking is weaker in both directions, because a check performed by the same process that made the error is not independent.

whyWrong.A: The tier change already produced an improvement in reasoning and wording, which is evidence the current tier is capable. Reverting to something stronger spends more to address a step that is unreliable at every tier.
whyWrong.C: Self-checking catches some errors and not others, and the ones it misses are the plausible ones. It also adds tokens to every monthly run without changing the fact that the calculation happened inside the same generation.
whyWrong.D: Rounding does not verify anything, and hedging with a confidence flag on a simple arithmetic step adds noise without a mechanism. If the flag is not shown, nothing changes; if it is, someone still has to check every figure.

questions.mindset: Keep the tier that improved the reasoning; remove the unreliable step rather than exhort against it.

questions.stem: A 40-person operations department runs Claude for roughly 80% routine work — formatting, summarising, first-draft replies — and about 20% work that feeds external commitments: customer quotations, regulatory returns and incident write-ups. They exhausted last quarter's allowance in week three, and two incidents came from routine work rather than the high-stakes category. The department head asks you to set a tier policy. Which TWO statements would make the policy sound? Choose TWO.

options.text: Set a default fast tier for routine work and require the strongest tier only for a named list of high-stakes tasks, so cost tracks value rather than habit.
Review the split periodically: the work mix changes, new model versions change what the routine tier can do, and allowance limits do not.
Require everyone to use the strongest tier, so nobody has to think about which category a task falls into.
Ban the fastest tier for routine work, since routine work still reaches customers.
Let each person choose freely, since only they know how important their work is.

questions.explanation: A policy for a mixed workload has to answer two questions — **what goes to the capable tier** and **when the answer changes** — and the two correct options are those. Option A prices the work by value rather than by habit, which is what makes 80% of the volume affordable and keeps the strongest tier available for the 20% where a reasoning error is externally visible. It also avoids the failure mode in the question: routine work reaching customers is a **review and verification problem, not a tier problem**, and it is solved by requiring a person to check anything that leaves the department. Option B is what makes the policy durable rather than a one-off decision — model capability at a given price changes with releases, and allowance limits are finite, so a policy written once and never revisited will quietly become wrong.

whyWrong.C: This is the policy that produced the exhaustion in week three. Avoiding a classification decision is a poor trade when it means paying for the strongest capability on work where it adds little and running out of allowance before the month is out.
whyWrong.D: Banning the fast tier removes the only mechanism that makes high volume affordable, so the allowance problem gets worse and the routine work is not made safer by an upgrade. The two incidents described were verification failures, which this change would not have prevented.
whyWrong.E: Unguided choice produces exactly the inconsistency the department already has. Without a named high-stakes category and a stated default, usage will drift to the most capable tier by habit, which is what exhausted the allowance.

questions.mindset: Set a cheap default and a named high-stakes exception, and revisit the split when models or limits change.

questions.stem: A sales manager is 80 messages into a chat about a complex tender response, and it has been going well. She now needs to draft a two-paragraph internal note about holiday cover for her team, which has nothing to do with the tender. What is the MOST appropriate thing to do?

options.text: Start a new chat for the holiday note, so the tender context does not interfere with it and the note does not fill the tender conversation.
Continue in the same chat, because Claude already understands her and the context will make the note better.
Ask Claude to summarise the chat first, then write the note in the same conversation.
Ask Claude to forget the tender material before writing the note, so it does not appear.

questions.explanation: Unrelated work in an established chat is a **context hygiene** problem in both directions. The tender material occupies most of the history, which makes it more likely to bleed into a short internal note; and the note itself is clutter in a conversation that may run several more days and may need to be handed to a colleague. Starting a fresh chat costs one message and keeps each piece of work clean — and her personal working preferences still apply across her chats, which is the reassuring part of this advice. The alternatives each add a step without solving the issue: summarising the chat creates a summary that is context for the wrong task, and asking Claude to forget something mid-conversation is not a reliable control.

whyWrong.B: Knowing her well does not help when the task is unrelated, and the accumulated tender context works against her here. The likely result is a note that refers to bid language, deadlines or customer names that have no business in a holiday rota.
whyWrong.C: Summarising is the right tool when continuing the *same* work, which is exactly why it is wrong here. It produces more history to work through in order to write something unrelated.
whyWrong.D: Forgetting is not a dependable mid-conversation control, and it is aimed at the wrong thing. The problem is not that tender content will leak into the note, it is that the note does not belong in this conversation at all.

questions.mindset: One chat, one piece of work — unrelated tasks deserve a fresh chat, and summarising is for continuing, not starting over.

questions.stem: A data team's monthly reporting notes have accumulated four months of decisions in a single chat: which measures were chosen, why two were dropped, and the exact definitions used. Next month two analysts will run the report instead of her, and the definitions must be identical. What is the MOST effective use of Claude's features?

options.text: Ask Claude to remember the definitions, so it applies them automatically in every conversation from now on.
Print the chat and file the printout with the reporting instructions.

Ask Claude to write the decisions and definitions into a Project as instructions and a knowledge source, so every future chat in it starts from the agreed rules and can be updated by whoever owns the report.
Keep the chat going and tell the new analysts to read through it before starting.

questions.explanation: The requirement here is **shared, durable and maintainable**, and those three words point to a Project. Shared matters because two other analysts must work from exactly the same definitions; durable matters because the rules need to outlive a single conversation and survive staff changes; maintainable matters because next quarter's definitions will change and someone has to be able to find and edit them. A Project separates **instructions** (how to do this report: the measures, the definitions, the format) from **knowledge** (the source material itself), which is precisely the split that makes the setup editable. A chat fails the shared and maintainable tests, memory is personal rather than team-wide, and a printout is neither searchable nor updateable.

whyWrong.D: Asking people to read a long chat is the manual version of the problem. Definitions will be read differently, nothing is authoritative, and next month's amendments have nowhere obvious to go.
whyWrong.A: Memory is a personal feature applied across the user's own chats. It is not a team-shared, version-controlled place for report definitions, and it is the wrong home for exact figures that must be identical every month.
whyWrong.B: A printout is frozen the moment it is produced and cannot be searched or updated in place. It also cannot enforce anything, so the first question asked next month will produce a fresh answer.

questions.mindset: Shared, durable, maintainable knowledge belongs in a Project; a chat and memory are neither shared nor editable.

questions.stem: An operations lead has worked for two weeks in one long chat on a warehouse relocation plan. The chat has become unwieldy, so he asks Claude to summarise everything so far and continue from the summary. The new plan carries forward the correct overall sequence but restates the agreed cost ceiling as 'about £400,000' when the figure agreed with the landlord was £365,000 plus a break clause he is relying on. What does this MOST usefully tell him, and what should he do?

options.text: Summaries preserve the shape of a conversation but not its exact figures and conditions, so exact terms must be restated from the source document when work continues in a new chat.
The summary process is unreliable, so he should abandon long chats and return to a series of short questions.
The figure has been lost permanently and cannot be recovered, so he should reconstruct the lease terms from memory before continuing.
He should ask Claude to summarise the summary to confirm the figure is stable, and continue once two summaries agree.

questions.explanation: Summarisation is genuinely useful for carrying **structure** forward — the sequence of work, the decisions taken, what is still open — and this is why it is the right tool here. What it does not preserve is **exact figures and their conditions**, because a summary is a paraphrase by design. That is the behaviour to expect rather than a defect to work around, and the practical rule follows: anything exact or conditional gets restated from the source document. Note the compound risk in the example: a figure has been approximated *and* the break clause attached to it has dropped, which is the kind of detail that quietly changes a plan. Option B throws away the structural benefit for a problem the summary approach largely solves.

whyWrong.B: Short chats would remove the long-history problem by removing the history, which throws away two weeks of accumulated context and reasoning. The sequencing came through correctly, which shows the summary did its job.
whyWrong.C: The figure is recoverable from the lease and from the earlier chat, and reconstructing it from memory is precisely the risk here. A wrong break clause in a relocation plan has consequences the rest of the plan depends on.
whyWrong.D: Summarising a summary is a second lossy pass, not a check. Agreement between two summaries of a paraphrase tells her nothing about whether either matches the lease.

questions.mindset: Summaries carry decisions and structure forward but not exact figures — restate anything precise or conditional from the source.

questions.stem: A policy analyst answers a different question about the same 120-page staff handbook every day, and has started pasting the entire handbook into each new chat so Claude always has the full text available. She has noticed the answers about later sections have become vaguer, and the pasted text is now a significant part of every conversation. What is the MOST effective change?

options.text: Keep the handbook as a knowledge source in a Project, keep the Project instructions brief and specific to her role, and ask focused questions so only the relevant material is in play for each one.
Split the handbook into four chats, one per quarter of the document, and use whichever chat the question seems to belong to.
Move to the most capable tier, since the handbook's length is making the later answers worse.
Summarise the handbook at the start of each chat, then paste the summary instead of the full text.

questions.explanation: This is the **context-as-substrate** problem: material that should be available on demand has become permanent payload in every message. That is why answers about later sections are deteriorating — with the whole document in context, attention and useful relevance are spread thin, and the query competes with a large body of text it does not need. Option A fixes the cause by separating **what is always available** (the handbook, as a knowledge source in a Project) from **what is always in the prompt** (brief role-specific instructions and one focused question). It also makes the material updateable in one place when the handbook is revised. The distractors are worth understanding: splitting by section guesses at relevance, a stronger tier does not change how a long input is attended to, and summarising first is a second lossy pass over material she needs verbatim.

whyWrong.B: Section-based chats require her to guess which quarter contains the answer, and policy questions routinely span sections. A question answered from the wrong chat is worse than a vague answer, because it looks authoritative.
whyWrong.C: Model capability is not the bottleneck described here. The issue is how much material is competing for attention in every message, which is a matter of what she pastes, not which tier answers.
whyWrong.D: Summarising a policy handbook and working from the summary risks exactly the failure mode above: an approximation of a document whose wording is the whole point. She would be reasoning about a paraphrase to answer a question that turns on precise clauses.

questions.mindset: Material that is always needed should be available on demand, not pasted into every message.

questions.stem: A six-week capital project has produced a decision log with exact figures and conditions: which supplier was chosen, the committed dates, the approved budget lines and two conditions the board attached to its approval. The project lead is leaving, a new lead starts on Monday, and the board expects the log to be authoritative at its next meeting. Which TWO statements BEST describe how the knowledge should be held? Choose TWO.

options.text: The log belongs in a Project as a knowledge source, so it is shared, current and available to whoever works on the project.
It should also be kept as a living document the team edits directly, so amendments are made in the document itself rather than argued over inside a chat.
It should be held in the outgoing lead's personal memory, since that is what memory is designed to retain.
It should be kept only in the original chat, since a chat is a complete record of everything that was decided.
It should be summarised into a brief overview, since the board only needs the headline decisions.

questions.explanation: The requirements are **shared, exact and living**, and the two correct options address them separately. Option A handles shared and current: a Project is where material belongs when more than one person needs it and it must be updated in one place, and it applies automatically to every chat in the Project rather than depending on someone remembering to paste it. Option B handles the nature of the artefact: a decision log is a document that is amended, so people need to edit it directly rather than negotiating changes through conversation — which is what makes it authoritative at the board meeting. The alternatives each fail one of the requirements plainly. Memory is personal and leaves with the person, so option C is the wrong owner for institutional knowledge. A chat is not a complete record — it is the place where knowledge is most easily lost and hardest to review. A brief overview discards the exact figures and board conditions, which are the parts the board will check.

whyWrong.C: Memory is personal to one user and would leave the organisation with the outgoing lead. The new lead could not rely on it, and nothing in it would be auditable or correctable by the team.
whyWrong.D: A chat is not a reliable record of decisions: content gets summarised as chats grow, it is hard to navigate and impossible to amend in place, and the original wording of a figure or condition can quietly change.
whyWrong.E: A headline summary is the wrong level for an artefact the board will treat as authoritative. Exact figures and the conditions attached to approval are precisely what gets checked, and they are what a brief version drops first.

questions.mindset: Shared knowledge goes in a Project; anything that gets amended over time belongs in a document people can edit directly.
